[1] I bought my first cello at forty-one, from a shop that smelled like varnish and old carpet. The owner asked how long I had played. I told him the truth, which was never, and he did not laugh, he simply handed me a rental contract and a cake of rosin. For a week the instrument sat unused and unplayed in its case by the door, and I walked past it the way you walk past a task you have promised someone else you will do.

[2] My teacher, Ms. Okonkwo, taught mostly children. [A] Her studio held a shelf of small violins, a poster of the circle of fifths, and a corkboard covered in the childrens' recital programs. [B] She never once suggested that I was too old, though I raised the subject at nearly every lesson, hoping to be excused in advance. [C] Instead she gave me exercises so slow that the effort of them was totally in the waiting. [D]

[3] What surprised me was how much of the difficulty was not musical. A child learning the cello is learning to sit still and hold a bow; an adult learning the cello is learning to be bad at something in front of a witness. Cellos have been built in roughly their present form since the sixteenth century. I had spent twenty years becoming competent at one job, and competence, it turns out, is a habit that resists interruption.

[4] Progress, when it came, arrived in pieces too small to celebrate. One month the open strings stopped buzzing. Another month my left thumb quits gripping the neck as though the cello were trying to escape. Watching my bow arm in the studio mirror, my elbow dropped whenever I stopped paying attention. By spring I could play a two-octave scale slowly and in tune, and hearing it I felt something closer to relief than triumph.

[5] I am not going to claim that the cello made me a better person. It made me a worse cook: I practiced during the hour I once spent on dinner. What it gave me was narrower and stranger than improvement: forty minutes a day in which I was unmistakably a beginner, and in which being a beginner was the entire point.

[2] The method itself is plain. Whitefish steaks, small potatoes and onions go into a kettle of salted water suspended over a wood fire outdoors. Salt does most of the work: it seasons the fish, and it raises the density of the water so that the oils cooked out of the whitefish come up on top. [A] Near the end, the boilmaster throws kerosene on the fire. [B] The flames surge, the kettle erupts, and a sheet of oily foam goes over the rim and into the coals. [C] What is left in the kettle is clean. [D]

[3] Visitors film the boil-over. Residents, who have seen several hundred of them, tend to watch the boilmaster instead. The timing is not obvious: too early and the fish is underdone, too late and it has gone to threads in the water. The kerosene is a tool, not a garnish, however the show it produces is real, and nobody involved pretends to be embarrassed by it.

[4] The tradition is younger than most menus suggest. Fish boils were a way to feed a crew — lumber camps, church suppers, a fleet coming in, cheaply and outdoors, and the commercial version dates from the middle of the twentieth century, when restaurants along the peninsula began charging admission to something families had did for free. Purists call this a loss. It is at least an odd kind of preservation: a chore that survived by becoming a performance.

[5] I have eaten the result perhaps a dozen times. It is good and not remarkable — firm fish, salt, melted butter, boiled potato. What is remarkable is the twenty minutes before it, standing in a semicircle in the cold with strangers, all of us waiting for a fire to do something. The food is the reason given. The fire is the reason.

[1] The co-op began, as most of its members tell it, with a dispatcher who quit. In the spring of 1994 the city's largest courier company cut its riders' commission from sixty percent to fifty. Which the woman who answered the radio would not accept. Eleven riders left with her. They had no office, no insurance, and no clients; what they had was a dispatcher who knew every account in the city by voice.

[2] For the first four months the business ran out of a rented room above a bicycle shop, with one phone line and a corkboard. [A] Riders paid in a flat weekly fee that covered the phone, the rent, and the dispatcher's wage. [B] Everything a rider earned beyond that fee was the rider's to keep. [C] The arithmetic was the whole argument: at the old company a rider handed over half of every fare; at the co-op a busy rider handed over almost nothing. [D]

[3] Governing the co-op was harder than funding it. The members wrote their bylaws in a single evening and then spent the next six years after that amending them. Who gets the good runs on a slow day? What happens to a member who breaks a collarbone in November? Early on such questions were settled by whoever was loudest; by 1999 there was a written rota, a hardship fund, and a rule that any member could call a meeting with two days' notice.

[4] The work itself never got easier. Riders were hit by cars, doored, and ticketed. Winter took a third of the roster most years, and the co-op survived by being cheap to run rather than because it was comfortable to belong to. Its files, which a member donated to the city archive in 2016, are mostly ledgers: fares, dues, and a column headed “owed.”

[5] Fax machines, then email, then a courier app took most of the small work away, and by 2011 the co-op had ten members and one contract, ferrying blood samples between two hospitals. It closed in 2014 with money in the account, which its last members considered a decent result. The dispatcher, who was the first to leave the old company and the last to leave this one, kept the corkboard.
